rejected.title: Relativity in action
card: Muons

Muons are made high in the atmosphere and last only about 2.2 microseconds at rest. In that time they could not travel far enough to reach the ground, yet many do. In Earth's frame the muon's clock runs slowly, and in the muon's frame the trip is shorter.
Accelerators
Particles in accelerators move very close to the speed of light. Their design must use relativity, or the predicted behaviour of the particles would not match what is measured.
GPS

GPS satellite clocks tick at a different rate from clocks on the ground. Their speed slows them by about 7 microseconds a day, while weaker gravity at their height, an effect of general relativity, speeds them up by about 45. Without corrections, timing and position errors would build up each day.
In each case, measurements match relativity and do not match the predictions of Newton's mechanics.
rejected.remember: Muon survival, accelerator design and GPS timing all match relativity, not Newton.

a.q: Many muons made high in the atmosphere reach the ground. What is the best explanation?
opts: Their short lifetime is stretched in Earth's frame
Their lifetime is longer in the muon's own frame
Their speed is greater than the speed of light
Earth's atmosphere slows them so they last longer
a.why: Measured from Earth, the muon's clock runs slowly, so it lasts long enough to reach the ground. In its own frame its lifetime is still only about 2.2 microseconds, so the option about the muon's own frame is wrong.
a.clue: The 2.2 microsecond lifetime is measured with the muon at rest.

b.q: An engineer says GPS needs relativistic corrections. Which statement best supports this?
opts: Without corrections, satellite clock errors would build up
Satellites travel faster than light relative to Earth
Satellites are too small for Newton's mechanics to apply
Radio signals from satellites travel at varying speeds
b.why: Satellite clocks tick at a different rate from clocks on the ground, because of both their speed and the weaker gravity at their height. Uncorrected, the timing errors would grow and cause position errors. The corrections are made to the clocks, not to the speed of the radio signals, so the option about varying signal speeds is wrong.
b.clue: The corrections are about the clocks.

problems.detail: "At that lifetime they would travel too far to survive the trip" says the opposite of what is meant. At 2.2 microseconds they would not travel far enough: the trip is too long for them to survive.

The GPS line puts the need for corrections down only to the clocks moving fast. The larger GPS correction is the gravitational (general relativity) effect, about +45 microseconds a day, and it is opposite in sign to the speed effect of about -7 microseconds a day. The card should not imply that motion alone is the cause.

Why (b) says "the last option is wrong" about signal speed. In the order shown, the last option is the correct answer and the signal-speed option is second, so the why contradicts the question as students see it.
The clue "whose clock runs slowly in Earth's frame" repeats "Earth's frame" from the correct option and sets it apart from the muon's-own-frame distractor, which nearly gives the answer away.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. Why (b) calls the correct option "the last option" and wrong, and the clue for (a) nearly gives its answer away.
